title: People can value smartphones while struggling to reduce their use
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey of U.S. adults

observations.period: May 26-June 1, 2026; smartphone time, perceived excess, and self-regulation

spend_too_much_time.unit: percent of adults answering the smartphone-time item

tried_to_cut_back.unit: percent of U.S. adults in the prior-12-month question frame

cutback_extremely_or_very_successful.unit: percent among adults who tried to cut back

cutback_somewhat_successful.unit: percent among adults who tried to cut back

cutback_not_successful.unit: percent among adults who tried to cut back

observations.method: Pew American Trends Panel survey using self-reported smartphone-time judgments and retrospective attempts to reduce use; displayed item denominators vary by question and exclude nonresponse where noted.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not use device logs, identify the product or app involved, or measure duration, dependence, clinical harm, or actual behavior change after the survey.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; adults ages 18-49 were more likely to report trying to cut back than older adults, while reported success varied little by age among those who tried.
observations.counterinterpretation: Failure to cut back may reflect social, work, safety, navigation, or information needs rather than simple lack of willpower; perceived excess can coexist with useful or necessary phone functions.

observations.period: May 26-June 1, 2026; smartphone utility and perceived cost

denominator.unit: U.S. adult survey respondents; item-specific response bases apply

observations.method: Descriptive survey items on perceived smartphone benefits and costs; the measures are not combined into a net-wellbeing score.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived information, connection, productivity, and sleep effects are not clinical or behavioral measures and do not establish that smartphone use caused the reported outcome.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with age differences reported for several utility and cost measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same device can provide connection or information while creating distraction or sleep costs; the tradeoff may differ by work, care, age, safety, and social setting.

related_sources.claim: Pew's topline supplies question wording and item-specific response bases.

boundary: This record identifies a perceived-usefulness, perceived-cost, and self-regulation gap. It does not establish device-logged exposure, addiction, clinical harm, platform causation, durable behavior change, political action, or successful digital exit.
